Regression and Correlational Analysis¶

Regression Analysis¶

Regression analysis is a statistical technique used to examine the relationship between one or more independent variables (predictors) and a dependent variable (outcome). It helps to understand how changes in the independent variables are associated with changes in the dependent variable. Regression analysis can be used for prediction, forecasting, and identifying important factors that influence the outcome.

History of Regression Analysis¶

The term "regression" was first introduced by Sir Francis Galton in the late 1800s when he observed that the heights of children tended to regress toward the mean height of their parents. Karl Pearson and Ronald Fisher further contributed to the development of regression techniques in the early 20th century, leading to its widespread use in economics, social sciences, and natural sciences.

Correlation Analysis¶

Correlation analysis measures the strength and direction of the relationship between two variables. Correlation does not imply causation; it only indicates the presence and strength of a relationship.

In [1]:

import warnings

1. Explore the Dataset (mtcars)¶

The mtcars data was extracted from the 1974 Motor Trend US magazine, comprising fuel consumption and 10 aspects of automobile design and performance for 32 automobiles.

url_mtcars = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vincentarelbundock/Rdatasets/master/csv/datasets/mtcars.csv"
mtcars = pd.read_csv(url_mtcars, index_col=0)

Scatter Plots are Essential Before Regression and Correlation¶

Note: There is a strong negative correlation between weight and miles per gallon. As the weight of the car increases, the miles per gallon decreases.

In [6]:
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.regplot(x='wt', y='mpg', data=mtcars, 
            scatter_kws={'color': 'blue', 's': 20}, 
            line_kws={'color': 'red'})
plt.title("Relationship between Weight and MPG")
plt.xlabel("Weight (1000 lbs)")
plt.ylabel("Miles per Gallon")
plt.show()

Compute Pearson & Spearman Correlation Analysis¶

Hypotheses:

  • H0: There is no significant correlation between weight and miles per gallon ($r = 0$).
  • H1: There is a significant correlation between weight and miles per gallon ($r \neq 0$).

Decision Rule: If the p-value < 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis.

Pearson Correlation¶

In [7]:
r_pearson, p_pearson = stats.pearsonr(mtcars['wt'], mtcars['mpg'])
print(f"Pearson r: {r_pearson:.5f}, p-value: {p_pearson:.2e}")

Pearson r: -0.86766, p-value: 1.29e-10

Spearman Correlation (Non-parametric, used when normality is violated or data is ordinal)¶

In [8]:
r_spearman, p_spearman = stats.spearmanr(mtcars['wt'], mtcars['mpg'])
print(f"Spearman rho: {r_spearman:.5f}, p-value: {p_spearman:.2e}")

Spearman rho: -0.88642, p-value: 1.49e-11

2. Simple Linear Regression (SLR) - mtcars¶

Equation: $\hat{MPG} = 37.2851 - 5.3445 \times wt$

Interpretation: For every 1 unit increase in weight (1000 lbs), the MPG decreases by ~5.344 units.

Fit Simple Linear Regression¶

In [19]:
model_slr = smf.ols('mpg ~ wt', data=mtcars).fit()

3. Hypertension Data (SLR with Missing Data Handling)¶

We will load htn_dat.csv, check for missing values, perform complete case analysis (drop NA), and model SBP ~ BMI.

In [ ]:
try:
    htn = pd.read_csv("htn_dat.csv")
    print("--- Missing Values Summary ---")
    missing_vals = htn.isnull().sum()
    display(missing_vals[missing_vals > 0]) # Show only columns with missing values
    
    # Complete case analysis
    comp_data = htn.dropna()
    
    # Scatter plot
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
    sns.regplot(x='BMI', y='SBP', data=comp_data, 
                scatter_kws={'color': 'steelblue'}, 
                line_kws={'color': 'red'})
    plt.title("Relationship between BMI and SBP")
    plt.show()
    
    # SLR Model
    model_htn = smf.ols('SBP ~ BMI', data=comp_data).fit()
    print(model_htn.summary())
    
    # Predict for new patient: Weight=75kg, Height=1.75m
    bmi_new = 75 / (1.75**2)
    new_person = pd.DataFrame({'BMI': [bmi_new]})
    pred_htn = model_htn.get_prediction(new_person).summary_frame(alpha=0.05)
    print(f"\nPrediction for BMI = {bmi_new:.4f}:")
    display(pred_htn[['mean', 'mean_ci_lower', 'mean_ci_upper', 'obs_ci_lower', 'obs_ci_upper']])
    
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("[Note] 'htn_dat.csv' not found in directory. Skipping Hypertension section.")

Model Diagnostics: Multicollinearity & Influential Observations¶

  • VIF (Variance Inflation Factor): Values > 5 or 10 indicate high multicollinearity.
  • Cook's Distance: Identifies influential observations. Threshold commonly set at $4/n$.

1. Multicollinearity (VIF)¶

In [25]:
X_vif = mtcars[['wt', 'hp']].copy()
X_vif['const'] = 1 # VIF requires the constant term
vif_data = pd.DataFrame()
vif_data["feature"] = X_vif.columns
vif_data["VIF"] = [variance_inflation_factor(X_vif.values, i) for i in range(X_vif.shape[1])]
print("--- VIF Values ---")
display(vif_data)

--- VIF Values ---
feature VIF
0 wt 1.7666
1 hp 1.7666
2 const 12.1615

2. Cook's Distance & Influential Observations¶

In [26]:
influence = model_mlr.get_influence()
cooks_d = influence.cooks_distance[0]
mtcars['cooks_d'] = cooks_d
threshold = 4 / len(mtcars)
influential_obs = mtcars[mtcars['cooks_d'] > threshold].index
print(f"\nInfluential observations (Cook's D > {threshold:.3f}): {influential_obs.tolist()}")

Influential observations (Cook's D > 0.125): ['Chrysler Imperial', 'Fiat 128', 'Toyota Corolla', 'Maserati Bora']

3. Refit without influential observations¶

In [27]:
mtcars_no_inf = mtcars.drop(influential_obs)
model_mlr_no_inf = smf.ols('mpg ~ wt + hp', data=mtcars_no_inf).fit()
print("\n--- MLR Model Summary (No Influential Obs) ---")
print(model_mlr_no_inf.summary())

Inferential Tests for Assumptions¶

  1. Normality: Shapiro-Wilk & Anderson-Darling tests.
  2. Homoscedasticity: Breusch-Pagan test.
  3. Independence: Durbin-Watson test.
In [28]:
residuals = model_mlr.resid

1. Normality Tests¶

In [29]:
stat_sw, p_sw = stats.shapiro(residuals)
print(f"Shapiro-Wilk Test: W={stat_sw:.5f}, p-value={p_sw:.5f}")

stat_ad, crit_ad, sig_ad = stats.anderson(residuals, dist='norm')
print(f"Anderson-Darling Statistic: {stat_ad:.5f}")

Shapiro-Wilk Test: W=0.92792, p-value=0.03427
Anderson-Darling Statistic: 0.66581

Q-Q Plot & Histogram¶

In [30]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
sm.qqplot(residuals, line='s', ax=ax[0])
ax[0].set_title("Q-Q Plot of Residuals")
sns.histplot(residuals, bins=10, kde=True, ax=ax[1], color='steelblue')
ax[1].set_title("Histogram of Residuals")
plt.show()

2. Homoscedasticity (Breusch-Pagan)¶

In [31]:
bp_test = het_breuschpagan(residuals, model_mlr.model.exog)
print(f"\nBreusch-Pagan Test: BP={bp_test[0]:.5f}, p-value={bp_test[1]:.5f}")

Breusch-Pagan Test: BP=0.88072, p-value=0.64380

3. Independence (Durbin-Watson)¶

In [32]:
dw_stat = durbin_watson(residuals)
print(f"Durbin-Watson Statistic: {dw_stat:.5f}")

Durbin-Watson Statistic: 1.36240

Diagnostics for Log-Log¶

In [36]:
resid_log = model_econ_log.resid
stat_sw_log, p_sw_log = stats.shapiro(resid_log)
print(f"\nShapiro-Wilk Test (Log-Log): W={stat_sw_log:.5f}, p-value={p_sw_log:.5f}")

bp_test_log = het_breuschpagan(resid_log, model_econ_log.model.exog)
print(f"Breusch-Pagan Test (Log-Log): BP={bp_test_log[0]:.5f}, p-value={bp_test_log[1]:.5f}")

Shapiro-Wilk Test (Log-Log): W=0.96678, p-value=0.00000
Breusch-Pagan Test (Log-Log): BP=71.28804, p-value=0.00000

6. Additional Macro Example (CPI & Elasticities)¶

Modeling Consumer Price Index (CPI) against Exchange Rates and Lending Interest Rates.

Log-Log Equation: $\ln(CPI) = -0.7043 + 1.5149\ln(ExchRate) - 0.5520\ln(LendIntRates)$

In [38]:
try:
    df_macro = pd.read_csv("training model.csv")
    
    # Standard MLR
    model_cpi = smf.ols('CPI ~ ExchRate + LendIntRates', data=df_macro).fit()
    print("--- CPI MLR Summary ---")
    print(model_cpi.summary())
    
    # Cook's Distance & Refit
    inf_cpi = model_cpi.get_influence()
    cooks_d_cpi = inf_cpi.cooks_distance[0]
    df_macro['cooks_d'] = cooks_d_cpi
    thresh_cpi = 4 / len(df_macro)
    inf_obs_cpi = df_macro[df_macro['cooks_d'] > thresh_cpi].index
    df_macro_no_inf = df_macro.drop(inf_obs_cpi)
    
    model_cpi_no_inf = smf.ols('CPI ~ ExchRate + LendIntRates', data=df_macro_no_inf).fit()
    print("\n--- CPI MLR Summary (No Influential Obs) ---")
    print(model_cpi_no_inf.summary())
    
    # Log-Log Elasticity Model
    model_cpi_log = smf.ols('np.log(CPI) ~ np.log(ExchRate) + np.log(LendIntRates)', data=df_macro).fit()
    print("\n--- CPI Log-Log Elasticity Summary ---")
    print(model_cpi_log.summary())
    
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("[Note] 'training model.csv' not found. Skipping CPI section.")

7. Demand Analysis (Double-Log Model)¶

Because both dependent and independent variables are in logarithms, coefficients are interpreted as elasticities.

  • Price Elasticity: -1.139 (Elastic demand)
  • Income Elasticity: 0.753 (Normal necessity)
  • Cross-Price (Substitute): 0.537 (Substitute goods)
  • Cross-Price (Complement): -0.407 (Complementary goods)
In [40]:
try:
    df_demand = pd.read_csv("demand_data.csv")
    model_demand = smf.ols('np.log(Quantity) ~ np.log(Price) + np.log(Income) + np.log(SubPrice) + np.log(CompPrice)', data=df_demand).fit()
    print("--- Demand Analysis Log-Log Summary ---")
    print(model_demand.summary())
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("[Note] 'demand_data.csv' not found. Skipping Demand Analysis section.")

8. Consumption and Income Example¶

Estimating the impact of Income on Consumption. We will also estimate a Long-Run Consumption Model by forcing the intercept to zero (- 1 in the formula).

In [41]:
try:
    df_income = pd.read_csv("income.csv")
    
    # Simple Linear Model (with intercept)
    model_cons = smf.ols('Consumption ~ Income', data=df_income).fit()
    print("--- Consumption ~ Income SLR Summary ---")
    print(model_cons.summary())
    
    # Long-run Consumption Model (No Intercept / Forced through origin)
    model_cons_lr = smf.ols('Consumption ~ Income - 1', data=df_income).fit()
    print("\n--- Consumption ~ Income Long-Run (No Intercept) Summary ---")
    print(model_cons_lr.summary())
    
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("[Note] 'income.csv' not found. Skipping Consumption and Income section.")
